candidates.title: Build the node with fat LTO and codegen-units=1 (env-only; thin LTO as the cheaper variant) so the hot FixedPoint and torus-core helpers inline across crates
candidates.mechanism:
There is no [profile.release] in the workspace Cargo.toml or in .cargo/config.toml. Every bench node is therefore built with codegen-units 16 and only thin-local LTO, so non-generic, non-#[inline] functions cannot be inlined into another crate. The hot cases are:
- torus-types FixedPoint: from_raw, raw, checked_add/sub/mul/div and the Add/Sub/Mul/Div/AddAssign/SubAssign impls (lib.rs:158-268). None has #[inline], and rustc's automatic cross-crate inlining does not apply because they call the panic path through expect().
- torus-core helpers called from torus-bridge and torus-consensus: margin::order_initial_margin :65, mark_loss :125, placement_need :161, order_price_violation (order_book.rs:518), AccountMargins::get (order_book.rs:756), position::signed_size.
- The __rust_alloc / __rust_dealloc / __rust_no_alloc_shim allocator shim.

The profile shows these as standalone symbols called from other crates; for example <FixedPoint as Sub>::sub is a 64 B function called from torus_bridge, torus_core and torus_consensus.

The premise of the task is wrong for borsh and alloy. Their hot paths are generic, such as <Order as BorshSerialize>::serialize::<Vec<u8>> and <[u8;20] as Hash>::hash::<FoldHasher>, so they are already compiled and inlined in the calling crate. The torus-state overlay methods (get_cf_raw, put_cf_raw_owned) do cross a crate boundary, but they are large, so inlining them saves little.

The experiment is env-only, with no repo edit:
- CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat
- CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1
- the thin variant is CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=thin with codegen-units left at 16
- panic stays unwind.

What it should change:
- LLVM inlines the 64-288 B callees.
- i128 values stay in registers instead of being passed by &mut through memory.
- Result values are no longer returned by sret.
- The calls and prologues disappear. archy's bench builds force frame pointers, so every such call currently also pays a push/mov/pop of rbp.

What LTO cannot remove:
- __divti3, the i128 division libcall from checked_mul and the margin helpers.
- glibc memcpy/memcmp.
- RocksDB, zstd and jemalloc, which are C/C++ (there is no cross-language LTO).
- Keccak, which is assembly.
candidates.evidence:
**Profile.** Source: 300m, current-era Phase 3/4 build d3cba5e2, an ancestor of main. Whole-process W1 run on val1: cycles:u at 499 Hz with frame-pointer call chains. Files: /home/oz/bench-results-matched/ozarchy-p4s0-run/analyst/p1-mperf-w1-all.script.gz and nm.txt. I parsed them read-only with /tmp/lto-scan/scan.py and fp.py.

Exec thread (17,912 samples, 11.1% of the process):
- FixedPoint self time 1.22%: checked_mul 0.60, AddAssign 0.25, Sub 0.21, Add 0.09, SubAssign 0.07.
- Small (≤320 B), non-generic cross-crate leaf functions total 2.12%. Examples: order_initial_margin 0.39% (144 B, called from torus_bridge); AccountMargins::get 0.25% (288 B); order_price_violation 0.11%.
- Allocator shim 0.28%.

Exec pool (29,371 samples, 18.2%):
- FixedPoint self time 4.05%: checked_mul 1.49, AddAssign 1.28 (80 B, from torus_bridge), Sub 0.44, Mul 0.42, Div 0.23.
- Small cross-crate leaves 2.79%.
- Allocator shim 0.18%.

Not removable by LTO: __divti3 is 1.31% of exec and 2.59% of pool samples.

The 10m Phase 4 profile shows the same pattern: <torus_types::FixedPoint>::checked_mul is 0.70% of all cycles and <FixedPoint as Sub>::sub 0.20% (ozarchy-p4soak10-run/analyst/perf/top-b-k1-b.txt).

**Discount.** The exec thread is memory-bound: IPC 1.18 (15.71M instructions / 13.28M cycles per 1k fills) and 33k DRAM fills per 1k fills (docs/perf/bench-archive/tools/ozarchy-p3cloidprof-tools/analyst/llc.txt). So I counted only 0.6-0.8 of the call overhead as removable, and added caller-side spill savings of 1.2-2x the callee self time.

**Arithmetic, 300m 600 s on main.** Exec wall is 312 ms per native block, of which 268 ms on-CPU; the match and pass_a pool phases are 42 ms.
- Exec on-CPU: -1.5 to -3.4%, i.e. -4 to -9 ms.
- Pool phases: -2.3 to -5.4%, i.e. -1 to -2.3 ms.
- Total -5 to -11 ms per block (-1.6 to -3.7%).
- At exec busy 0.995 this gives matched/s of about +1.6 to +3.8%. The plan's rule of thumb (~0.3% per ms at 313 ms blocks) gives +1.5 to +3.4%.

**Upstream precedent.** reth, a dependency of this repo (checkout eb4c15e):
- Cargo.toml:282-304: its release profile is already lto=thin; its maxperf profile is fat LTO + codegen-units 1.
- docs/vocs/docs/pages/installation/source.mdx: maxperf 'improves some benchmarks by around 20% compared to release'.
- .github/workflows/release.yml:90: x86_64 releases use '-C target-cpu=x86-64-v3 -C target-feature=+pclmulqdq'.
candidates.est_gain:
Fat LTO with codegen-units 1, on top of the CRC arm (see the second candidate):
- 300m (exec-bound): exec block_ms -1.6 to -3.7%, i.e. -5 to -11 ms per native block in 600 s cells and -3.4 to -8 ms in the 120 s gate cells (211-226 ms blocks). Exec wall per 1k fills goes from 4.37 to about 4.21-4.30 ms. matched/s and native blk/s rise about +1.5 to +3.7% (central +2.5%). The margin, settle pass_b and match sub-timers should drop most, about 3-5% each.
- CPU-s/1M: about -1 to -2.5% (23.38 -> about 22.8-23.1). Estimated per thread as exec 11.1% x 1.5-3.4%, pool 18.2% x 2.3-5.4%, rpc and tokio about 1.5-3%, verify pools 0.5-1.5% (Keccak is assembly, k256 mostly already inlined inside its own crate).
- 10m: at tail depth 1 matched/s changes about 0 to +1.5%, because the bench tail sets the pace; CPU-s/1M again -1 to -2.5%. At depth 4 the gain is like 300m.
- RSS: about 0.
- Thin LTO alone: about 70-85% of the fat gain, because ThinLTO imports small functions such as the FixedPoint ops.
- Optional arm V (adds -C target-cpu=x86-64-v3 -C target-feature=+pclmulqdq): about 0 to -1% exec and -0.3 to -1% node CPU more (k256 field multiplies with BMI2 mulx, wider inline copies). Keccak (sha3-asm build.rs:98-108 uses the scalar x86_64 perlasm unless avx512vl), zstd (runtime BMI2, the ZSTD_*_bmi2 symbols are in the profile) and jemalloc do not change.
candidates.determinism:
Codegen only; no logic changes.
- State arithmetic is integer FixedPoint (i128): torus-types lib.rs:140-148, order_book.rs:9 'All arithmetic via FixedPoint (no f64)'. f64 appears only in metric gauges (liquidation_step.rs:231,343,532).
- LLVM keeps integer semantics. Rust never contracts floating-point operations into FMA.
- Exec hash maps are seeded per process (order_book.rs:13-15), so nothing can depend on iteration order today.
- Panic unwinding is kept, so catch_unwind containment and the fail-stop hook behave as now. panic=abort must never be used.
- The only theoretical risk is latent undefined behaviour in unsafe code that more aggressive inlining could expose. AGREE in every cell is the check.
- An optional mixed-fleet cell (one node built with LTO) would need a per-node BIN; devnet/wsl/env.sh:14 has a single BIN.

candidates.risks:
- **Build cost (inferred, not measured).** Baseline full build: 2m48-2m57s, 548 crates, jobs=16 (ozarchy-*-build logs); the binary has 27.9 MB of .text. Fat LTO + codegen-units 1 is estimated at 10-25 min with a single-threaded LTO stage and 8-16 GB peak RAM. Thin LTO is estimated at 4-7 min and +1-3 GB. archy has 62 GB with about 51 GB free. The fat build holds the shared build lock that item 7's builders also wait on, so schedule it with 18c.
- **Gain may be smaller than estimated.** The exec thread is memory-bound (IPC 1.18), so the gain could sit at the low end. +1.5% is just resolvable at n=4.
- **Bench vs production.** Bench builds force frame pointers, so the bench gain slightly overstates the production gain (production builds have no frame pointers).
- **Profiling.** perf output becomes coarser because more is inlined. The sub-phase timers are unaffected.
- **Latent undefined behaviour** could surface under heavier inlining; AGREE in every cell guards this.
- **Arm V portability.** It needs AVX2 (Haswell 2013+, AMD Excavator 2015+). Do not use target-cpu=native: it is non-portable and adds aes, which switches ahash's algorithm. ahash is only a transitive dependency here, randomly seeded, so there is no consensus effect.
- **Unwinding.** Never set panic=abort.

candidates.title: Compile RocksDB with hardware CRC32C (CXXFLAGS -msse4.2 -mpclmul, build env only) to shorten the ~0.6 s checkpoint batch write and the commit-persist write
candidates.mechanism:
librocksdb-sys 0.17.3 (RocksDB 10.4.2) decides on hardware CRC at compile time, and its build.rs:117-149 passes -msse4.2/-mpclmul only when CARGO_CFG_TARGET_FEATURE contains sse4.2/pclmulqdq.
- Without __SSE4_2__, crc32c.cc:252-271 uses the table-driven DefaultCRC32 (slicing by 4).
- crc32c_3way needs both __SSE4_2__ and __PCLMUL__ (crc32c.cc:1116-1125, which notes 'runtime detection no longer supported on x86').
- Bench and README builds use the x86-64 baseline target, so every WAL byte is checksummed in software.
- Every RocksDB LOG on current-main cells says so: 'Fast CRC32 supported: Not supported on x86', for both the state DB and the consensus DB (/home/oz/bench-results-matched/ozarchy-hsdb-300m-r2-B/rocksdb-LOG-val1.txt and rocksdb-consensus-LOG-val1.txt).

The expensive WAL writes all use the default WriteOptions, so the WAL is on:
- the ~200 MB checkpoint batch the flush worker writes (backend.rs:2194 -> StateDb::write, db.rs:1158);
- the 3-12 MB block body that the consensus thread's persist_committed_block_durably writes as one WriteBatch (app.rs:1449-1460, called from dispatch_to_exec);
- the DA put_batch calls (native_da.rs:304).

Pipelined writes are on, so the checkpoint batch's WAL append, including its CRC, sits at the head of the state-DB write queue that section 74 blames for the in-window stall.

The fix is env-only: CXXFLAGS_x86_64_unknown_linux_gnu="-msse4.2 -mpclmul".
- cc-rs reads this variable; the librocksdb-sys build output lists it among its rerun-if-env-changed probes.
- RocksDB is the only C++ dependency. It is compiled by GCC 16 via c++; the repo's CXX_librocksdb_sys entry in [env] is not a cc-rs variable and has no effect.
- So only the RocksDB (and bundled snappy) objects change. The Rust code generation is identical to main.
- CRC32C values are identical between hardware and software, so the WAL and SST formats do not change. SST blocks already use XXH3 (table.h:283, format_version 6).

candidates.title: Settle pass A: split one heavy market's plan into trader shards (maker releases by order id, taker releases by order range), with an optional sub-flag that computes each plan inside its market's match job
candidates.mechanism:
Today pass A packs whole markets into LPT chunks (native_executor.rs:8631-8713), and compute_market_settle_plan walks one market's orders and fills serially (8947-9046). A market is the smallest unit. When one market carries s of the flow, its plan is one job of about s x 150 thread-ms per call, and that job sets the length of pass A.

The plan is not price-time sequential:
- A position key is (trader, market), so a trader's transitions depend only on that trader's earlier fill sides (position.rs:550-580, 796-832).
- cum_volume is a per-trader sum (add_fill_volumes, native_executor.rs:215-223).
- The taker release is a pure function of each order (10082-10094).
- Maker releases aggregate per maker order id, and their output order is the BTreeMap order of those ids (9239-9300).

Split a market whose fills >= MIN into K shards. Shard k does three things:
- (a) It applies the fill sides whose trader hashes to k, in the original fill order, into its own PositionCache and VolumeCache.
- (b) It aggregates the consumed and STP maps for maker order ids with id % K == k.
- (c) It computes taker releases for order index range k.

Merge:
- The K position caches and volume maps are disjoint by trader. Pass B merges each part with merge_disjoint (8774-8789) and iterates each volumes map (8909-8912).
- pnl_events are k-way merged per order by `at`.
- Maker releases are k-way merged by order id, consumed list first, then STP, which reproduces the BTreeMap order exactly.
- If any shard returns a fill_error or panics, or a cached row names another key (the update_in_place cross-key branch), that market is recomputed unsharded with today's function. Fallback and fault precedence (8719-8766) are therefore unchanged.

Sub-flag TORUS_FUSED_MATCH_PLAN=1: compute each market's plan at the end of its match job (market_workers.rs:336-384), from the same inputs (post-match book, results, prepared orders, the backend frozen from 7434 to the cache flush). The exec-thread steps between match and pass A (7771-7796: sort, TraderMarkets/CloidMarkets absorb, clearing the reduce-only and account-margin state, counters) never change orders or positions. As a result:
- the light markets' plans run hidden behind the hot market's matching;
- pass A's separate fork-join and its 3-4 ms pool start latency disappear;
- the hot plan's shards go to the idle pool threads through a nested exec_pool::run_jobs, which works because rayon scope runs in place on a pool worker.

Plans are discarded if use_parallel turns out false (7802-7817).

candidates.determinism:
This changes scheduling only, and every node computes byte-identical state.
- Each (trader, market) position key is advanced by exactly one shard, in the original fill-side order, so the union of the disjoint caches equals the unsharded cache. flush_all sorts the keys anyway.
- Per-trader volume sums keep their addition order.
- Taker releases are pure per order.
- Maker releases aggregate each order id over its fills in the original order (first-seen maker and price kept, STP last-write) and are merged by id, which reproduces the BTreeMap iteration order the A5 clamps in pass B see.
- pnl events are merged by (order, at).
- A shard error, a shard panic, or a cross-key row triggers an unsharded recompute of that market with today's function. The existing fallback and fault-latch logic therefore sees an identical plan set.
- Fusion computes the same pure plan from the same inputs. The steps it moves the plan ahead of touch no orders and no positions, and plans are dropped when use_parallel is false.
- Match panics stay fatal (run_contained). Plan panics stay recoverable (catch_recoverable).
- The flag is node-local: validators with mixed settings agree.

TORUS_PASS_A_SHARDS=K:

result.summary:
The premise holds on main a44000e0 and the gain arithmetic holds at 100% cloid share. The problem is the regime: the gain exists only when orders carry cloids. Code facts checked on main:
- The duplicate pre-pass (native_executor.rs:7318-7367) runs after the phase1 timer stops (:7316) and before the margin timer starts (:7375).
- The post-match CloidMarkets::absorb loop (:7776-7781) runs after the match timer (:7757) and before the settle timer (:7797).
- The stash drain (:5344-5352) is called at app.rs:4036, after save_books, with no timer.
- All three run serially on the exec thread.
- exec_pool::run_jobs has only two callers: match (market_workers.rs:183) and pass A (native_executor.rs:8698). The pool is idle at all three points.
- Since 0be7d6ae, the only commits that touch the cloid code are the O(1) index-guard fixes (a18ae28b, 95872049, 8d4f00f5). So section 63's profile of F100 (bc44a845, the code that was merged) still applies.

Measured, removable from the exec thread at c100 (300m, 120 s): drain 0.140 + pre-pass 0.154 = 0.294 ms CPU per 1k fills, about 13.4 ms per native block at 45.6k fills. The pre-pass figure is 0.167 minus the count loop (at most 0.013), which stays.

The parallel version leaves a residual of roughly 0.05-0.14 ms per 1k fills:
- each of the 8 jobs filters the full list (about 64k placements, about 80-115k drain records);
- the exec thread waits for the slowest of the 8 jobs;
- 2 fork-joins on a host where 3 nodes share 32 hardware threads.

Net saving: about 0.15-0.24 ms per 1k fills, central about 0.20.
- Section 63's calibration is -0.285 ms per 1k fills = +5.6% matched/s at busy 0.96.
- That puts the gain at c100 at about +4% (+3.0 to +4.7%), against the candidate's +4.4 to +5.0%.

The headline gain only exists at 100% share:
- c50: about +2%.
- c25: about +1%, below the n=4 CI of about ±1.3%.
- c0: exactly 0. CloidMarkets is never built (it stays None), the pre-pass is skipped because cloid_places == 0, and absorb only clears empty logs.

c0 is the harness default (CLOID_SHARE unset means no cloids, run-cell.sh:88-92), the Phase gate shape and every latency and soak campaign. There is no CPU-s/1M benefit (the work is moved, not removed), RSS is flat, and nothing in the change acts on block p99.

The data back the c100 gain: the removable cost is measured on the same code, and section 63 measured how exec-thread cloid savings turn into matched/s. Only the parallel efficiency is unmeasured. So: keep, but rank it as a gain that depends on cloid share. Do not compare its +4.5% with candidates whose gains are measured at c0.

Value is only above noise at high cloid share. It cannot pass the standard Phase gate template at c0, because nothing changes there. The owner must accept a gate that depends on cloid share before an M-sized change to the exec hot path is merged.

Before building:

result.summary:
Keep it, with must-fix constraints. I found nothing that makes lazy custody unsafe for determinism or consensus. The main problem is the recovery claim: on multi-body misses, serving shards makes recovery slower than custody=0, not faster.

Why it is safe:
- Shards are not consensus state. The only production reader of cf_native_shards is the shard serve (swarm.rs:376), and the erasure root is not committed to consensus in Phase A (shard_recovery.rs:39).
- A recovered body is kept only if it decodes and re-hashes to the hash the block references. Since F-2 that hash covers the full signature (torus-types lib.rs:1170-1215), so no node can absorb a different body.
- Every production write to cf_native_pending goes through put or put_batch, which store canonical bincode. So get_raw returns exactly the bytes eager custody would shard, and encode() is a pure function of (bytes, k, n). Lazy and eager shards are byte-identical.
- On the consensus thread, lazy is exactly the existing TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0 early return (app.rs:6722). That path covers all three call sites and the async-validate worker, and every bench cell already runs it with AGREE.

Problems found:
1. **New remote panic.** On a miss, the derive would index with the peer-chosen shard_index. merkle_proof and StoredShard::from_encoded_body panic when the index is out of range. The spawn_blocking serve closure releases its DaServePool slot only after the call returns. So 8 bad requests from any peer (banned peers are served too) would permanently turn off all body and shard serving on that node.
2. **Slow recovery consumer.** Lazy brings the shard recovery path back into use, and that path costs O(M x S). recover_bodies_via_shards calls try_reconstruct_from_shards for each missing hash over the whole pool. Each call re-verifies every pooled shard and trial-reconstructs every complete group, because a response carries no body hash. On a full-block miss at 300m (about 359 bodies, about 718 shards of ~10 KB), that is an estimated 3-15 s before the whole-body pull even starts. Today's custody=0 costs 500 ms plus the pull. Under 3/3 quorum that node's MissingData votes hold up commits. The same flaw is already latent in the production default (custody=1).
3. **The proposed crash/rejoin cell never reaches the new code.** Block sync pulls whole bodies only (app.rs:6291-6316).
4. **custody=0 already gives the whole hot-path gain, with zero code.**
result.corrected_gain:
**Bench as configured (custody=0):** 0 by construction, for matched/s, CPU and I/O alike.

**Against the production default (custody=1):** the mechanism is real but the saving is unmeasured.
- Custody runs synchronously on hotstuff-algo, before the proposal on the leader and before the vote on followers, at all three call sites. It also writes cf_native_shards.
- The +12% matched/s central estimate is a model only; the zero-code step 0 pair has to establish it.

**Against custody=0:** about 0 extra matched/s. TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0 (gate A1, 8fa6ccd, the bench default) already removes all of the hot-path cost with zero code.
- Lazy's only addition is shard availability during recovery.
- That is a net loss on multi-body misses (an estimated 3-15 s per full 300m block versus about 0.5 s plus the pull) until the recovery consumer is made linear.
- It is a small win only for misses of a few bodies, where it skips today's 500 ms empty pre-step.

Reported number: 0 (bench as configured; also the expected gain over custody=0).
result.constraints:
1. **Flag unset must equal main.** Use one shared parse and OnceLock (in torus-state) for both torus-consensus and torus-network.
   - Trimmed "0" means off; trimmed "lazy" means lazy.
   - Everything else stays eager exactly as today: unset, "", "1", "true", "off", and any other string. See /home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs:592-597; the test at :629-638 pins "true" and "" as on.
   - Move and extend that test.

2. **Hot path.** Under lazy, return at the same point as custody=0 inside custody_native_shards_core (app.rs:6720-6724): after the ObserveOnDrop span, before ErasureParams and mirror_native_shards.
   - That covers the proposer (:6648), the full-block path (:6825), the compact path (:6896) and the torus-async-validate worker.
   - Do not touch mirror_or_drop_native, the fail-closed body mirror or the MissingData paths.

3. **Serve gating.** In /home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-network/src/swarm.rs serve_native_da_shard (:358-393), derive only when the mode is lazy and get_shard returned Ok(None).
   - Eager and off modes keep today's present=false on a miss.
   - Read the validator count only in lazy mode.

4. **No panics on peer input.** Check before any indexing:
   - validator count 0: answer present=false;
   - params = ErasureParams::for_validator_set(count);
   - shard_index >= n: answer present=false;
   - encode errors (n > 255; k == n when n <= 2, because ReedSolomon::new(k, 0) errors): answer present=false;
   - no unwrap or expect anywhere on this path.
   - Reason: merkle_proof and StoredShard::from_encoded_body index without checks (/home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-state/src/erasure.rs:225-240, /home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-state/src/shard_store.rs:52-61).

5. **Panic-safe slot release.** Release the DaServePool inflight slot with a drop guard (or catch_unwind) in the spawn_blocking shard closure. Today it is decremented only after the call (swarm.rs:2111-2119). Otherwise 8 panicking requests from any peer permanently stop all DA body and shard serving on that node.

6. **Locks.** Read shared.validators.read().len() on the swarm loop with no other lock held, drop it before spawning, and pass a plain usize into the closure.
   - Never nest it with peer_map.
   - Reason: is_validator_peer (swarm.rs:685-690) already takes peer_map then validators, the reverse of init_validator_set / update_validator_set (/home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-network/src/bridge.rs:622-663). That is a pre-existing ABBA deadlock risk; do not add to it.

7. **Byte-identity tests.**
   - A derived StoredShard has the same bytes as encode_stored_shard(StoredShard::from_encoded_body(encode(get_raw bytes, for_validator_set(n)), i)), for n in {1,3,4,7,21}. n <= 2 must give present=false, the same as eager custody failing today.
   - The levels-once proof equals merkle_proof(shards, i) for every i.
   - Body lengths {0, 1, odd, 20489}.
   - serve_shard_out_of_range_index (swarm.rs:4331) must stay green in lazy mode with the body stored.

8. **Serve budget.** Derived serves must not crowd whole-body serves out of the shared 8-slot pool (MAX_DA_SERVE_INFLIGHT, swarm.rs:613). Give derives their own small budget or cache EncodedBody per body. Record native_da_serve_dropped in every cell.

9. **Fix the recovery consumer first.** This must happen before claiming any recovery benefit, or before using lazy anywhere custody=0 is the alternative. Make recover_bodies_via_shards (app.rs:5080-5145) and try_reconstruct_from_shards (/home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-consensus/src/shard_recovery.rs:41-88) linear:
   - attribute each shard response to its body hash (map OutboundRequestId to the hash, or add body_hash to the response);
   - verify each shard once, on arrival;
   - keep a pool per body and drop shards for bodies no longer missing;
   - discard late shards left over from earlier cycles (the queue holds up to 10k);
   - or skip the shard pre-step above a small M.
   Add a test with M = 359 realistic 20 KB bodies and 2M shards, with a wall-time bound.

10. **Test plan.** The crash/rejoin cell does not reach the derive path: block sync uses pull_missing_bodies, then recover_bodies_bounded, which pulls whole bodies only (app.rs:6291-6316). Add a forced hot-path push-miss cell or test (drop the pre-proposal push to one follower for N blocks). Check AGREE, native_da_shard_recovered, recovery wall time and commit freezes.

11. **A/B arms.** Add custody=0 as an arm next to custody=1 and lazy. Lazy has to beat custody=0 on something other than hot-path cost.

result.summary:
KEEP. I found nothing that could make nodes disagree. The change only swaps RocksDB's internal CRC32C (used for WAL and MANIFEST integrity checks) from the software table path to the hardware path. CRC-32C is a fixed function, and I checked the two paths give the same output on this exact compiler. I compiled RocksDB 10.4.2's own util/crc32c.cc three ways: software, SSE4.2-only, and SSE4.2+PCLMUL (crc32c_3way), all with GCC 16.2.1 at -O3. All 87,329 outputs matched byte for byte. They covered every length from 0 to 4,200 bytes at offsets 0-15 (63,744 cases are above the 216-byte 3-way threshold), buffers from 32 KiB to 8 MiB, and 20,000 Extend-chaining checks; the standard check value e3069283 came out right. The scratch files are in /tmp/claude-1000/crc32c-equiv-s124.

Rust code generation does not change, for three reasons: cc-rs 1.2.60 reads CXXFLAGS_<target> only for C++ compiles, bindgen 0.72.1 ignores it, and librocksdb-sys (with its bundled snappy) is the only C++ crate built on Linux. With the variable unset, the binary is main's binary. The bench cells and consensus see no protocol or ordering change, only shorter write durations, which were already reachable timings on a shared host.

The issues are about measurement and deployment, not determinism:
- Bench cells use fresh data dirs, so they never read back a WAL or MANIFEST CRC. AGREE therefore cannot catch a CRC defect, so a restart check is needed.
- Production builds would crash with SIGILL on CPUs or VM CPU models that lack PCLMULQDQ.
- Every A/B in archy's paused queue must use the same build flag in both arms.

On the paused work: this candidate has no code overlap with the 4 paused exp/s123 branches or with 18c's slicing branch. It only shifts the build baseline.

result.summary:
I could not refute this candidate on determinism or safety grounds, so keep it. Both arms can be made byte-identical to main.

Why the parity holds:
- **What the trailing verify actually does.** In ecdsa 0.16.9 recover_from_prehash, the trailing verify recomputes X = (z/s)G + (r/s)Q, and with Q = r^-1(sR - zG) that is exactly R. x(R) mod n is r for every recid, so the verify can only fail on k256's own low-S check (k256 0.13.4 ecdsa.rs:201-208). An explicit is_high() check therefore reproduces today's accept set exactly.
- **libsecp256k1 edges.** I read sig_recover in secp256k1-sys 0.11.0. Every edge matches k256: r, s in [1, n-1] (k256's parse runs first anyway); recid 2/3 rejected exactly when r >= p-n = 0x14551231950b75fc4402da1722fc9baee; non-residue x and an identity result rejected by both; z reduced mod n by both; the same y-parity rule; the same uncompressed keccak address.
- **Where a parity bug would bite.** The trust cache is keyed by the full signature (torus-types lib.rs:1247-1261). It is seeded only by the gossip and RPC paths that recover the sender themselves, and exec trusts its hits without re-verifying (app.rs:3372-3395). A parity bug would therefore change exec state, and whether it showed would depend on timing. That is why the low-S check and the parse order are mandatory.
- **Votes and timing are unaffected.** No consensus or timing code changes. validate_block does no per-action ecrecover; the attested path checks one ed25519 signature. Votes, timeouts and view changes are untouched. Nothing is persisted, so crash and restart under either flag value replay through the same parity.
- **Concurrency.** The secp256k1 0.31.1 global context is set up once behind std::sync::Once and is read-only after that. Its rand-based randomization only blinds signing, never recovery.

The remaining risks are implementation discipline, listed under constraints: panic-free code, parse order, and arm-pinned tests. The candidate does not touch any of the four paused s123 branches. Its only neighbour is a textual one: exp/s123-exec-action-keys-parallel edits eip712.rs around lines 1075-1336, while ecrecover is at 807-823.

result.constraints:
1. **Check order in every arm:**
   - k256 Signature::from_slice, mapping failure to InvalidSignature;
   - then RecoveryId::from_byte(v.wrapping_sub(27)), mapping failure to InvalidSignature;
   - then bool::from(k256_sig.s().is_high()), mapping high-S to RecoveryFailed (use k256's own predicate, s > (n-1)/2, not a hand-written constant);
   - then the arm's recovery, with every failure mapped to RecoveryFailed.
   Putting the low-S check before the recid parse would change the RPC error text for a high-S signature with a bad v. Exec and the oracle-signer proof (native_executor.rs:11981) use .ok(), so error variants only reach RPC text.

2. **Flag unset is today's code.** Unset, empty or unknown TORUS_ECRECOVER must run today's VerifyingKey::recover_from_prehash call, byte for byte. Parse the flag once with a pure parser plus a OnceLock, like parse_parallel_verify (eip712.rs:1094-1114). Log the effective arm once at startup, or export it as a gauge, so every cell proves which arm ran.

3. **libsecp256k1 arm uses the safe API only:**
   - RecoverableSignature::from_compact;
   - SECP256K1.recover_ecdsa(Message::from_digest(hash.0), &sig);
   - keccak256(serialize_uncompressed()[1..]), then the last 20 bytes.
   No raw ffi. No expect or unwrap: revm's RecoveryId::try_from(..).expect must become a map_err. The reasons:
   - The gossip-verify pool's spawn has no panic handler (torus-node main.rs:834-873), so a panic aborts the node.
   - Past 1,024 queued verifies, ingest runs inline on the tokio gossip loop, so a panic there silently kills gossip ingest.
   - libsecp's illegal-argument callback aborts. The safe wrapper keeps it unreachable.

4. **Dependency.**
   - Add secp256k1 0.31 (=0.31.1, the same version as revm-precompile 32.1.0), with only features that build already enables: recovery and global-context. Never lowmemory or global-context-less-secure. That keeps one libsecp build, which already decides EVM ecrecover results.
   - torus-types is also used by the tools (bench-throughput, wallet, faucet, price-feeder). They will now compile libsecp's C code. The cc and perl prerequisites already exist for sha3-asm, and there is no wasm target.

5. **Tests.**
   - Pin the arm explicitly, e.g. ecrecover_with(mode, ..), mirroring batch_verify_native_actions_cached_with_mode. The OnceLock cannot be flipped inside one test process.
   - The k256 reference stays compiled in the default arm. KATs a-j and the fuzz compare (variant, address) against it.
   - Random fuzz essentially never reaches recid 2/3 or r near p-n (probability about 2^-128), so the constructed edge cases are mandatory. I checked the candidate's expectations: x=1, x=n+2 and x=p-3 are on the curve; x=5 is not.
   - The high-S twin (s' = n-s, v xor 1) must also be tested end to end:
     - add_native_action_from_gossip with claimed sender = signer is rejected on every arm;
     - the twin's verified_cache_key never enters the trust cache;
     - batch_verify_native_actions_cached_with_mode returns None for it.

6. **k256-noverify arm.**
   - It must mirror ecdsa 0.16.9 recovery.rs:286-310 exactly:
     - bits2field / reduce_bytes;
     - checked_add(ORDER), returning Err on overflow;
     - decompress with the y-parity bit;
     - NonZeroScalar invert;
     - u1 = -(r^-1 z) and u2 = r^-1 s;
     - lincomb, then from_affine (identity rejected).
   - The only change is skipping verify_prehash.
   - Keep the differential test against recover_from_prehash permanently, so any k256 or ecdsa upgrade re-runs it.

7. **Shadow arm.** k256 stays authoritative. Mismatches only increment a counter, with a rate-limited log; never assert or panic.

8. **Evidence order.**
   - The KATs, the differential fuzz of at least 10^7 cases and the batch differential must pass before any cell runs.
   - A mixed-fleet AGREE cell on bench traffic is only a smoke test. k256 signing normalizes s (ecdsa.rs:193-196), so the bench only sends valid low-S signatures and never reaches the edge cases.
   - Run a shadow soak with mismatches = 0 before enabling the arm on any non-bench validator. With 3/3 quorum and exec trusting cache hits, a parity bug would mean one node's state diverging, caught only by AGREE or the state-hash attestation.
   - Only one TORUS_ECRECOVER arm is active at a time, so the two arms can never be stacked.

The premise is true in code, but the gain cannot be confirmed from data, and it is zero on every configuration the bench measures. That is fatal for this as a perf candidate.

What holds in code:

Why there is no measurable gain:
- devnet/wsl/env.sh:56 pins TORUS_SHARD_CUSTODY=0. All 567 archy cells with a captured env (1,701 node envs) ran with 0.

- The recovery benefit is immaterial: 0-4 DA recovery handoffs per node per 600 s cell, on the off-thread worker, and 0 shard recoveries.

The +12% is measured against a custody-on baseline that has never been measured. My own estimate of the custody cost (about 95-145 ms per block per node) agrees with the candidate's 120-135 ms, but it is a model, not data. This candidate re-proposes s65 explorer erasure-da-prod idea 2, which was parked for the same reason.

The real finding is a gap between bench and production configuration. It needs a zero-code measurement and an owner decision on the production default, not a perf branch.

**Against the custody-on production default (never measured; my own recompute):**

Removed cost, 300m: about 95-145 ms per non-empty block per node, at about 1 call per block per node.
- Body size: bincode is 51 B per order, so a 400-order place is about 20.5 KB. About 234 places plus 125 cancel-alls gives about 4.8 MB per block.
- Keccak volume: 6 x 4.8 MB for the Merkle tree plus about 4.2 MB for the action rehash, about 33 MB per block.
- Keccak rate on archy under load: about 280-310 MB/s (exec verify takes 16.8 ms for about 4.2 MB of cache-key preimage). block_build_mirror takes 20-22 ms for the same bytes. The asm keccak bench (commit 82523da5) gave 276-305 MB/s. That puts keccak at about 100-120 ms per block.
- Other work adds about 15-30 ms: bincode writes the 7.2 MB of shard bytes one element at a time, plus the RS encode, a new ReedSolomon per action, clones and a 7.4 MB WriteBatch to the consensus DB.
- s64's estimate of 20-40 ms was too low.

CPU:
- hotstuff-algo on-CPU would rise from 61-62 ms per committed block today to about 160-205 ms. That is +0.30-0.45 cores per node.

Critical path:
- Custody adds about twice its cost per view (leader build plus the slowest follower's validate, with a 3/3 quorum): 190-290 ms.
- The slack available is about 150-190 ms per view, spent waiting on the exec send. On val2, on_committed_block takes 210-214 ms against 51-60 ms on val0/val1. The view is 311-315 ms; consensus work alone is about 125-160 ms.

- The candidate's central +12% falls inside this range, but no cell confirms it.

Device writes: about -22.8 MB/s raw plus compaction, relative to custody-on only.

result.summary:
KEEP, severity minor. A build-setting change cannot change node state in safe Rust unless the compiler is wrong. On a44000e0 I checked the ways it could slip, and each is ruled out or can be checked:
- Consensus arithmetic is i128 FixedPoint. f64 appears only in metrics, timers and tests.
- The exec maps are seeded per process. AGREE already holds across nodes with different seeds, so map iteration order is proven irrelevant.
- The workspace has almost no unsafe code.
- There are no link-time registration crates (inventory, linkme, ctor, typetag) and no #[no_mangle], #[used] or link_section items.
- No logic compares function pointers or vtables.
- With the env unset, the binary is main's binary.

The candidate's own determinism section is right but incomplete. Four gaps:
1. All three nodes run the same binary, so AGREE cannot show equality with main. A deterministic codegen difference would agree with itself. Proof needs the golden-digest tests built with the same profile and, before adoption, a mixed-fleet or cross-binary restart cell.
2. panic=unwind is load-bearing. One example: a panic in the recovered settle plan falls back to the sequential path. Under panic=abort, every node would crash on the same block.
3. Every thread runs on the 2 MiB default stack, and heavier inlining grows stack frames. An overflow is a SIGSEGV abort, not the controlled exit-70 path, and it would hit all nodes on the same block.
4. Optional arm V (x86-64-v3) gives the same results, but a non-v3 host can hit an illegal instruction (SIGILL) on any code path at any time, not only at startup.

None of these blocks the A/B. All four are constraints on the build and on adoption.

result.constraints:
1. Panics must keep unwinding. Use panic=unwind in every arm and in any permanent profile, leave CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_PANIC unset, and never copy reth's 'reproducible' profile (it sets panic=abort). Containment depends on unwinding at these points:
   - crates/torus-consensus/src/app.rs:4623: the execution loop's catch_unwind sets exec_failed, then crates/torus-node/src/main.rs:921-935 exits with 70.
   - crates/torus-bridge/src/exec_pool.rs:52: catch_unwind per job.
   - crates/torus-bridge/src/market_workers.rs:320.
   - crates/torus-bridge/src/native_executor.rs:8651: catch_recoverable, where a panic in the settle plan falls back to the sequential path.
   - crates/torus-state/src/db.rs:185.
   - The R01b hook at crates/torus-node/src/main.rs:1803-1841.

2. The control must equal main.
   - Control: a44000e0 built with only the archy bench env (RUSTFLAGS='-C link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold -C force-frame-pointers=yes', CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=line-tables-only).
   - Each arm adds only CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO and CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS, plus the CRC arm's CXXFLAGS if L is stacked on C.
   - Build from a clean worktree pinned to a44000e0, into a new CARGO_TARGET_DIR per arm (avoids the S428 stale-rlib trap).
   - Take the shared flock (/tmp/claude-1000/torus-suite.lock) and never build during a cell. CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=8 overrides the jobs=16 in ~/.cargo/config.toml.
   - Pin every cell with EXPECT_NODE_MD5. Reuse the md5-pinned bench-throughput; never build the client with the LTO env.

3. AGREE alone does not prove equality with main.
   - Before the A/B, with the arm's exact env, run `cargo test --release -p torus-bridge --test perf_equivalence_golden`. It holds the scenario A serial and engine digests and the scenario B liquidation digests, pinned against main.
   - Also run crates/torus-core/tests/keccak_backend_vectors.rs, torus-bridge parallel_settle_tests, engine_parallel_tests and account_margin_tests, torus-state state_tests, and the panic-containment tests (the main.rs fail-stop hook, exec_pool and market_workers).
   - Before adoption, run one mixed-fleet cell (val1 on the LTO build, val0 and val2 on main) or restart val1 from main's data dir onto the LTO binary. AGREE and liveness must PASS. devnet/wsl/env.sh:14 hard-codes one BIN, and start-node.sh plus test_harness.py require the restart to use the same argv as the launch, so this needs a small harness change.

4. Crash and rare paths, before adoption:
   - One 300m cell with CRASH_KILL_AT_S (crash gate PASS).
   - One section-72 liq2 cell. The standard shape is mostly cancel-alls and barely exercises liquidation or ADL.

5. Stack.
   - Nothing in crates/ or tools/ sets stack_size, so every std, rayon and tokio thread runs on the 2 MiB default.
   - Compare the largest stack frames (objdump `sub $N,%rsp`) of the LTO binary against the control, and flag any frame above about 64 KiB on exec or consensus paths.

6. Allocator. Confirm the LTO build still runs unprefixed jemalloc for both Rust and C++ (RocksDB): the startup jemalloc_version line and the torus_jemalloc_* metrics must be present.

7. Arm V (x86-64-v3 + pclmulqdq) is for the bench only.
   - It gives the same results: v3 has no AES, so ahash keeps its fallback path, and hardware CRC32C equals the software CRC32C on disk.
   - But a non-v3 host can hit SIGILL on any code path at any time. Production use needs a startup CPU-feature check that exits before the DB opens, or a hardware floor. Never use target-cpu=native.
   - Run the CRC change as its own arm first.

8. Adoption.
   - Use a named profile, as reth does with maxperf: inherits=release, lto=fat, codegen-units=1, with panic="unwind" written out. Do not edit [profile.release].
   - This keeps `cargo build --release` equal to main and keeps fat LTO out of test and CI builds.
   - Staging must copy target/<profile>/torus-node to the path env.sh expects, with md5 pinning.

9. Reading results. Inlining can shift time between sub-phase timers, so judge on matched/s, block_ms, engine ms per 1k fills and CPU-s/1M. Use perf --inline for profiles.

result.summary:
KEEP, severity minor. The premise holds on main a44000e0, and the removable cost is slightly larger than the candidate claims. The 400 PlaceOrderItem hashes take 1,200 of the ~1,306 Keccak-f permutations per recover:
- each 320 B preimage needs 3 permutations;
- ordersHash 95, typehash strings 3, final 1;
- domain separator 5 (recomputed on every call), signing hash 1, address 1.

They run serially in hash_place_order_batch (/home/oz/projects/torus-economy/Torus-hyperBFT/crates/torus-types/src/eip712.rs:363-382), on the gossip-verify and ingress-verify rayon pools only. On exec the trust-cache misses are about 0.

Measured item-hash Keccak on current main is 0.41-0.43 cores per node, 7.8-8.1% of the 5.28-core node CPU. The candidate said 0.39 cores / 7.6%. Two independent derivations agree:
- (a) profile share × main thread CPU × the permutation model;
- (b) s77's measured 620 us per struct hash under load × 722 place-action recovers/s/node from counters.

result.summary:
KEEP, severity minor. I could not refute the candidate. It swaps the implementation of one deterministic function: every PlaceOrderItem preimage is a fixed 320 bytes in 3 Keccak blocks, because the cloid is always encoded as clientOrderId + hasClientOrderId (eip712.rs:311-327, 350-382). A correct x4 path gives byte-identical digests on any mix of flag values and CPUs. It does not touch consensus timing, locks or persistent state, and flag unset can run today's loop unchanged.

One correction to the candidate's safety argument. It says exec uses the struct hash only on trust-cache misses, but a single wrong x4 digest on one node is a fork:
- Senders computed through this function on RPC ingress and gossip seed the exec trust cache, and exec reuses them on hits.
- Session actions are hashed on the exec thread in every block (eip712.rs:1327, phase 2, no trust cache).
- Restart replay starts with an empty trust cache, so it recomputes every sender through this function.

Exactness is therefore a consensus requirement. This is the same risk class as the merged asm-keccak backend swap, which was accepted with known-answer and differential pins.

Two further hazards set hard constraints:
- **A panic aborts the node.** Gossip verify runs in a rayon ThreadPool::spawn with no panic handler (torus-node main.rs:834-873; rayon aborts in that case). It hashes before the batch-size guard (mempool lib.rs:797-834), so the batch length is controlled by the peer.
- **The A/B would be confounded.** run-cell exports EXTRA_ENV into the same shell that starts bench-throughput and the oracle feed, and the bench signs every action through this function. A flag read inside torus-types would switch the bench client too.

All are fixable, so this is not fatal.

Side finding, unrelated to the candidate and to be confirmed with 18c: the EIP-712 PlaceOrder and PlaceOrderItem structs do not sign StopMarket.trigger or StopLimit.{trigger, limit}; only the type tag is signed (eip712.rs:311-334, 366-368). Anyone relaying a signed stop order can change those prices and still pass verification. Both findings are saved to memory.

2. Compute the enable decision once, in a single OnceLock<bool>: flag set AND is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2") AND a startup self-test that matches scalar on fixed distinct vectors, including a 401-order batch.
   - On a self-test mismatch: disable x4, log an error and export a metric. Never panic.
   - No code path may call the avx2 function without this decision; a SIGILL crashes the node.
3. Panic-free and length-agnostic for any orders.len(). Gossip ingest runs in a rayon spawn with no panic handler (torus-node main.rs:870), so a panic aborts the node. It hashes before the batch-size guard (mempool lib.rs:797-834).
   - Use chunks_exact(4), and send the remainder through the existing scalar loop.
   - Fixed-size stack arrays only; nothing on the stack sized by n.
4. Lane j of group g writes item 4g+j at the same offset in acc as the scalar loop does.
   - ordersHash, the batch struct hash, the signing hash and the remainder stay on today's scalar keccak256.
   - Never touch canonical bytes, compute_action_hash or verified_cache_key (torus-types lib.rs:1183-1261).
5. Unsafe and SIMD hygiene:
   - Gate the code with #[cfg(target_arch = "x86_64")].
   - Keep all vector code inside #[target_feature(enable = "avx2")] functions, and keep vector types out of the signatures of functions without that feature.
   - Preferred route: a safe [u64; 4] newtype implementing keccak 0.1.6's pub LaneSize trait, with keccak_p::<L4>(state, 24) called from one avx2 function. The only unsafe is that call, made after detection, and correctness then does not depend on whether LLVM vectorizes the code.

6. Derive the fixed preimage length from the field count as a constant, with a const assert that it fits in 3 rate blocks (at most 407 bytes). If the item type changes (for example to sign stop trigger/limit, which makes 384 bytes), the absorb layout must follow.
7. Default off; with the flag unset, run today's loop.

9. Microbench gate before any node A/B: at least 2x on item hashing, measured single-thread and with the SMT sibling busy.

result.corrected_gain:
Figures are per node, 300m, 600 s cells.

**CPU-s/1M: about -0.8 to -1.0% (23.38 -> about 23.15-23.2).**
- Software CRC costs about 0.20 CPU-s/1M on main, which is 0.8-1.0% of node CPU.
- The rate comes from the d3cba5e2 val1 profile: 0.874% of cycles:u samples, 2,781 MB of WAL written and 231 user CPU-s in the window, which gives 0.74-0.90 ns per WAL byte.
- Main writes about 263 WAL bytes per fill (state DB 33.6 MB/s plus consensus DB about 25 MB/s, at about 223k fills/s).
- Hardware crc32c_3way (about 0.13 cycles/byte) removes about 96% of that cost.
- This is resolvable at n=3 ABBA: section 74 resolved -0.165 CPU-s/1M with a pooled sd of 0.024.

**matched/s: about +0.4 to +0.7% at 300m (point +0.5%), about 0 at 10m.**
- The only CRC on the exec critical path is at epoch boundaries (height % 100 == 0).
- On the r2-B logs, the exec thread waits 520-533 ms (mean) in pipeline_barrier before each epoch block, while the flush worker writes a drain checkpoint of about 120 MB. The epoch block then runs 120-160 ms longer, because it flushes about 73 MB serially on the exec thread.
- That puts 0.15-0.23 s of CRC on the exec path per epoch of about 34 s.
- This is below the n=3 600 s CI (about ±0.85%) and the n=4 120 s CI (about ±1.3%), so it cannot be resolved.
- It disappears if an epoch-boundary fast path lands.

**Direct timers (low-noise means per call):**
- Checkpoint DB write: 0.605 s -> about 0.37-0.45 s (-25 to -39%).
- commit_persist_write: 7.7-8.4 ms -> about 3-4.5 ms (body is about 5 MB per commit).
- commit_persist: about 15 ms -> about 10-11 ms. hotstuff-algo is not the limiter, so this changes no headline metric.

**Block p99:**
- In-window: likely -10 to -60 ms. Shortening the batch write should roughly halve the remaining state-DB excess wait (0.21 -> about 0.09-0.12 s/s). That is not resolvable at n=4-5, where the per-cell sd is about 72-80 ms.
- Out-of-window: 0.

**Other:**
- RSS: 0.
- Restart: WAL replay up to about 1.5 s faster with the 2 GiB WAL cap.

result.summary:
KEEP, severity minor. Under the determinism and safety lens, sharding the cloid index by key and running the pre-pass and the drains per shard on the exec pool is sound, and it can be made byte-identical to main. One claim is wrong: the panic handling for a drain job. The fix is small.

Why the results cannot change:
- Every CloidMarkets operation works on one key at a time: build, add_live, add_book, forget_book, absorb, live (native_executor.rs:3287-3369). The index is only used inside native_executor.rs and is never hashed or persisted.
- A pre-pass verdict depends on only two things: (a) the key's index slot plus the book it names, which are fixed after phase 1, and (b) earlier placements with the same key (the claimed set). The order is fixed by or_else at 7347-7354: check live first, and claim the key only if it is not live. No key affects another key's verdict, so splitting placements by key and keeping flat order inside each job gives the same accept/reject set, the same messages and the same counters.
- drain_cloid_keys (order_book.rs:2495-2513) looks every record up in the book's current map. When the log is empty it uses the values the worker already resolved, which are current. So every record of a key in one book resolves to one value, and applying them twice changes nothing. Across books the order does not matter, because a cloid is live in at most one book (the pre-pass and the single-path check at 10127-10142 enforce this). So taking the records out and applying them per key gives the same index, as long as no book changes in between. The borrow checker guarantees that.
- The reject message names the market and order id. It is stored in action status, which is node-local and not hashed (action_status.rs:20). Accept or reject itself does change state, and that stays exact.
- OrderBook: Sync is already proven. Settle pass A shares &[MarketBatchResult], each holding a book: OrderBook, across exec_pool jobs (8622-8701). So the candidate's open compile-time risk is not a risk.
- run_jobs runs jobs only on torus-exec-pool-* threads, catches each job's panic, and those threads are not in the node's fail-stop list. So the serial fallback for the pre-pass works. It matches settle pass A's sequential fallback (8648-8737).

What is wrong: the candidate says a drain-job panic followed by resume_unwind on the exec thread "keeps today's failure class". It does not. resume_unwind never calls the panic hook. Today a panic during the serial drain fires the R01b hook on torus-execution, which exits with code 70 before anything unwinds (torus-node main.rs:1803-1840). Under the candidate, the hook fires on a pool thread and does nothing. The exec thread then unwinds without logging to execution_loop's catch_unwind (app.rs:4623), which sets exec_failed. The poller then exits up to about 450 ms later (main.rs:921-935). It is still a fail-stop, and nothing is written, because the ExecutionContext Drop skips the final checkpoint once exec_failed is set. But it runs Drop code during the unwind, which R01b was built to avoid. The fix is a one-liner. The real hazard is any variant that swallows the panic and keeps the index: by then the logs were already emptied, so the index would be missing adds, and a later duplicate would be accepted on that node only, which is a fork.

No consensus code is touched, and there is no change to timeouts, views or leaders beyond host CPU contention from up to 6 more fork-joins per block. Restart is unaffected: the index is rebuilt from the books after a load. Every node gets the same results whatever its N or MIN.

result.constraints:
1. One routing function, shard(&CloidKey), for every CloidMarkets method and for assigning keys to jobs. The single place path (10127-10142), modify (10478), return_matched_book (5521), reconcile_lent_book (4546), insert_order_book / forget_book (5467) and build all stay serial but route through it. Set S once per process (OnceLock) and never change it while ResidentInner carries an index. Use a power of two with a mask, so routing cannot panic.
2. Flag unset, N<2, or below MIN: run today's code with no mix computed (S=1 shortcut). Keep drain_cloid_keys unchanged for the serial path.
3. Pre-pass:
   - All placements of a key go to one job, in flat order.
   - Per placement, keep the exact order of 7347-7354: duplicate_cloid/live first, then claimed.insert only if the key is not live.
   - Each job owns its claimed set and its cloid_checks/cloid_books_probed counters; the counters are summed afterwards.
   - Check every job's result for Err before applying anything. On any Err, throw away all job outputs and run today's serial retain on the exec thread, not inside catch_recoverable.
   - Write results and the DuplicateCloid metric in flat order, and call retain only when there are rejects.
   - If any job body can run inline on torus-execution, wrap it in catch_recoverable, as pass A does at 8648-8651.
4. Drains:
   - OrderBook::take_cloid_records must bump log_drains exactly once per book, every time, like drain_cloid_keys (this keeps the s120 lend guard right). It returns the resolved records, the log keys, and whether the log was non-empty.
   - When the log was non-empty, the job must look up every record, resolved and logged, in the book's current map, as in drain_cloid_keys' else branch.
   - Apply each key's records in take order.
   - When the index is None, clear the logs and spawn no jobs. This keeps c0 at zero cost.
   - Never mutate a book between take and apply. Do not overlap the jobs with the rest of the post-match loop or with settle.
5. The post-match drain jobs must join before settlement, before run_triggered_stops (7888) and before the post_evm call's pre-pass (app.rs:3738-3739).
6. A drain-job panic must NOT use resume_unwind, and must never leave a partly updated index in place. Pick one of these:
   - (a) panic! on the exec thread, so the R01b hook exits 70. This is today's class.
   - (b) Latch ctx.fatal_error and return early. At the post-match site, do it like the match-worker panic (7733-7755); app.rs:3747 catches it. At the stash, invalidate the holder and add a take_fatal_error check after app.rs:4036 and before the overlay flush. The last check today is at 3992.
   - (c) Deterministic recovery: serially re-apply all taken records (each one is idempotent per key), or set cloid_markets = None so the next check rebuilds from the books (all books are present at the stash, and they are back before run_triggered_stops).
   Do not invalidate the resident holder and carry on, because the next block could reload books whose deferred pass-2 bytes are not written yet.
7. Tests first:
   - Use an explicit mode parameter, like execute_batch_engine_mode or cancel_mode. A OnceLock env cannot switch arms inside one test process.
   - Compare flag on and off for N in {2,4,8}, two values of S, and MIN=0. Compare per-call results including messages, DuplicateCloid counts, counter totals, and index snapshots: covering after each call, exact after the stash.
   - Cases from the candidate: cross-market cloid, cancel-all then reuse, stops with cloids, triggered stops, a book lent through order_book_mut, insert_order_book replacing a book, and the post-EVM call seeing the pre-EVM call's adds.
   - Plant a panic in one pre-pass job: the serial output must be identical. Plant one in one drain job: the chosen fail-stop or recovery path must run, and no partial index may survive.
   - Keep debug_assert_covers and the full-scan comparison in debug builds.
8. Bench: AGREE in every cell and zero panic lines. Also report consensus timeouts and hotstuff-algo runqueue wait, because the extra pool wakeups hit a shared 32-thread host.
9. Optional: seed the shard mix per process (allowed, because the index is node-local). With a fixed public mix, a sender can choose cloids that all land in one shard. That only degrades to serial speed, with no safety impact.

Refuted. The setup the candidate describes is real on main a44000e0:
- Both verify pools run at the default nice. No priority code exists anywhere in crates/.
- BORE is on.
- The exec thread loses 2.46-2.64% of its wall to run delay (about 8.4 ms per block).

The two mechanisms that carry the gain are contradicted by switch data I extracted myself. The source is p4j3-300m-p1 perf-sched.data (val1, 45 s, per-thread switch events).

1) BORE is not what drives the exec thread's waits. Preemption rate and wait time per ms of on-CPU time do not grow with burst length:
- Bursts of 8.4 ms up to more than 134 ms (BORE score 0 to 6): 1.3-1.7 preemptions per 10 ms and 1.8-2.2 ms wait per 100 ms of on-CPU time, flat.
- The highest rates are in the first 8.4 ms of a burst, where the penalty is 0: 2.4 preemptions and 4.8 ms wait.

2) Exec-pool workers are mostly preempted by their own node's pool threads (about 70% of identifiable switches), and by verify threads in only about 10%. So the claimed -3 to -7 ms from faster pool starts and fewer mid-chunk preemptions is unsupported.

What is left is the verify threads' share of the exec thread's run delay: about 30-40% of identifiable preemptors, at most 2.5-3.4 ms per block. Add at most 1-1.5 ms from pool and helper threads. Total about 2-5 ms per block, central about 3 ms, so about +1.0% matched/s at 300m. The candidate claimed -5 to -12 ms and +2%.

That central +1.0% is below the n=4 paired CI of about ±1.3%. No work is removed, so there is no CPU-s/1M benefit. p99 and RSS gains would not be measurable. The 10m gate shape (tail depth 1) would gain about 0. The effect is also specific to 3 nodes sharing one host.

result.summary:
KEEP, major. Determinism is safe. Nice changes only timing, and the exec result does not depend on the trust-cache state: a hit returns exactly what a fresh recover returns (eip712.rs:1279-1298), and session actions are never cached. The flag is node-local, so a mixed fleet is safe, and with it unset there is no setpriority call, so behavior equals main.

The scope is wrong for the gossip pool, though. It is not bulk-only work:

(1) Proposal bodies go through this pool. Pre-proposal full-body pushes and B1 forwards enter the same unbounded inbound channel as gossip (swarm.rs:1661-1675, bridge.rs:218, main.rs:870). Each job mirrors the body to DA first (mempool lib.rs:797). A follower waits only one 20 ms slice (RECONSTRUCT_RETRIES=1, app.rs:5509-5510, 6398-6465) and then votes MissingData, which fails the view. Current main already has a thin margin:
- 300m (hsdb r1-r3 B, 600 s): 6-8 MissingData handoffs per cell, and 9-23 DA waits per node averaging about 20 ms, which is the full slice.
- 10m depth 1: 36-47 waits per node and 51-60 timeouts.
Nicing the queue that delivers these bodies directly raises the risk of failed views.

(2) Niced threads would run DA put_batch on the consensus DB (native_da.rs:97-122). That DB is shared with HotStuff vote-state, insert and commit writes (kv_store.rs:160-188). A niced RocksDB write-group leader can therefore delay the vote. Also, mirror_to_da takes the batch out under the lock and writes it outside the lock (lib.rs:1352-1378). flush_da_mirrors returns 0 when the buffer is empty (1386-1394), so a batch held by a preempted niced writer is invisible to the consensus thread's flush-on-miss.

(3) Niced threads hold std locks, which have no priority inheritance, that the exec and consensus threads also take:
- da_pending, with action.clone() inside the critical section (1353-1354);
- the native pool write lock (979), against select and remove_committed;
- the trust-cache write lock (510), against the exec thread's per-action reads (app.rs:3395). This std RwLock blocks new readers while a writer waits;
- read_view (284), against the exec thread's publish (277, app.rs:2705).

The ingress pool is already clean: it only verifies inside install, and admission runs on the RPC task (torus.rs:762-839). This is fixable by niceing only the pure-CPU stage, not fatal.
result.corrected_gain:

Under the constraints, key keccak and ecrecover stay niced. The DA mirror work (clone, bincode, action-hash keccak, RocksDB write) and admission move to nice-0 threads. By inference that is roughly 15-30% of gossip-verify CPU, so the candidate's +1.5 to +3.5% is an upper bound.

Implemented as specified, with the whole gossip ingest niced, the late-body and MissingData path and the HotStuff write-queue coupling could turn three things negative: block p99, consensus timeouts, and 10m depth 1.

Central estimate: +1% matched/s at 300m (range 0 to +2%), low confidence. At 10m depth 1 it is neutral to negative until pushes and forwards are split off the niced queue.
result.constraints:
1. Niced scope: only the pure-CPU stage runs niced.
   - In gossip ingest, that is verified_cache_key and recover_sender.
   - The trust-cache lookup may stay niced as a sub-microsecond read, preferably try_read with a recover fallback.
   - These must run on nice-0 threads:
     - mirror_to_da (the da_pending Mutex, the clone inside it, and the size/age put_batch);
     - NativeDaStore::put_batch and its arrival notify;
     - admit_gossip and submit_native_action_inner: ingress_state() and state reads, the pool insert under native.write(), and publish_native_pool_size;
     - cache_verified_sender.
   - Suggested shape: mirror on the inbound tokio task, or hand it to a dedicated nice-0 DA writer, before gossip_verify_pool.spawn. Return (sender, key) from the niced job to one nice-0 admitter.
   - Never hold a lock while waiting on a niced result.

2. Body availability must not depend on niced scheduling.
   - Pre-proposal pushes, B1 forwards (PRE_PROPOSAL_BATCH_MARKER) and gossip copies must reach da_pending or the DA store without waiting in the niced queue.
   - A batch taken by a niced thread must never be in flight while flush_da_mirrors returns 0. Constraint 1 covers this by doing no flushes on niced threads.

3. No niced thread may write RocksDB. The consensus DB is shared with HotStuff writes (vote state is persisted before the vote is sent). The state DB is shared with the checkpoint batch and the commit manifest.

4. setpriority rules:
   - cfg(target_os = "linux") only. libc in torus-node is cfg(unix), and on macOS/BSD PRIO_PROCESS would nice the whole node.
   - Apply per thread (who=0 or the tid).
   - Treat N as an increment on the inherited nice value, clamp the result to 19, and never lower it. Under CAP_SYS_NICE a negative value would push verify above hotstuff-algo.
   - Parse strictly as 1..=19; anything else means off, with a warning.
   - The start_handler must not panic. In rayon-core 1.13, a panicking start_handler without a panic_handler aborts the process (registry.rs:375-383, 921-926). That would happen at boot for the gossip pool and at the first RPC submit for the lazily built ingress pool. Log errors once and continue.
   - Add the hook in torus-rpc for the private ingress pool. That crate has no libc today.

5. No thread creation from niced threads. Nice is inherited on clone, and tokio spawn_blocking spawns new blocking-pool threads from the calling thread.
   - Niced code must never call spawn_blocking or thread::spawn.
   - It must never be the first to touch a lazy pool: eip712 live_verify_pool, the exec pool, or the global rayon pool. All of these hold today.
   - Unit test: after both pools have run work, the global pool, the exec pool, live_verify_pool and a fresh spawn_blocking thread all report nice 0, the pool threads report base+N, and with the flag unset everything reports base.

6. RocksDB sub-flag:
   - kLow sets absolute nice 19 (port_posix.cc:268-271) on the process-wide default Env.
   - Its 3-thread LOW pool compacts both the state DB and the consensus DB, and those threads take the DB mutex and the manifest-writer slot.
   - Run it as its own arm; never bundle it with N=10.
   - Guard rocksdb stall micros, L0 file count and pending compaction bytes on both DBs.
   - Never use SCHED_IDLE.

7. A/B guards in every arm (300m 600 s ABBA n=4, plus 10m at depth 1 and depth 4):
   - torus_native_da_recovery_handoffs_total (main: 0-4 per node per 600 s);
   - torus_validate_block_da_wait_seconds count and sum;
   - consensus timeouts;
   - HotStuff vote_state_write, view_insert_persist and commit_persist p99, and on_committed_block;
   - block_build_select and mempool_remove_committed p99;
   - exec verify ms;
   - a new exec-only trust-cache miss counter (the current miss counter includes gossip first copies);
   - a gossip in-flight gauge and an inline-fallback counter (the inbound channel is unbounded);
   - RSS;
   - AGREE in every cell.

result.summary: The premise holds on a44000e0. Each pipelined block's positions are deep-copied into an ingress slice on the torus-ckpt-merge thread and held until the next checkpoint or barrier. The only reader of positions through the view is funded fallback 3, which is off on the bench. The gain is real but smaller than claimed, and the exec-thread part of the claim is wrong. The ~37 inline drops per interval checkpoint only lower Arc reference counts, because the previous published view still holds every slice. Perf on d3cba5e2, which has the same view and dropper code, shows the slices are freed by the dropper and RPC threads. The exec thread frees them itself only at epoch-boundary barriers, which costs about 0.05-0.2 ms per native block on current main. Corrected at 300m: CPU-s/1M -0.3 to -0.5%, RSS mean -0.15 to -0.3 GB, jemalloc allocated peak about -0.5 GB, matched/s about +0.05% (noise). Keep it as an RSS and CPU clean-up item. Production needs the owner's sign-off and the exact variant.

The bench sets TORUS_INGRESS_MIN_COLLATERAL=0 (devnet/wsl/env.sh:67), but the production default is 1 TRS (funded.rs:58 DEFAULT_INGRESS_MIN_COLLATERAL_TRS). result.refuted:
1. Claim: the exec thread frees ~37 slices inline at each checkpoint, -30 to -50 ms at checkpoint blocks, about -1 ms per native block.
- The inline drops in clear_view_blocks only lower Arc reference counts. CkptState.published and the mempool's view still hold every slice up to n-3; only the n-2 slice can really be freed there.
- Perf on d3cba5e2 (p4s0 p1/p2 W1 all-thread dumps, same view and dropper code): exec-thread samples under checkpoint_upkeep are 71/74 and 35/43 synchronous L merges, and only 2-5 are drops.
- A window's slices are freed in one old-ReadView drop, on torus-ckpt-drop (477/415 samples per 45 s) or rpc-worker (145/134).
- The exec thread frees them inline only at epoch-boundary barriers: pipeline_barrier -> discard::<ReadView>, 63/29 samples, 14-36 per barrier, about 20-50 ms. This happens because C' was just handed to the 2-slot dropper.
- On a44000e0 those barrier windows hold only 8-12 objects (100 heights is about 33 s, two 15 s intervals plus about 3 s). So the cost is about 0.05-0.2 ms per native block.
- The checkpoint upkeep of 25-205 ms is mostly the two synchronous L merges.

2. Claim: the slice clone plus free costs 10-15 ms per native block, from the 18c probe. The owner relabelled that probe "ranking only" (mem 829b0d0f). Perf gives about 2.3 ms for the clone plus about 2.8 ms for the slice share of frees per native block on d3cba5e2, so about 6.5-7.5 ms at current block sizes.

3. Claim: L is about 188 MB. That figure is the mean including short barrier windows of 100-130 MB. Full 15 s windows close with L at 245-265 MB.

4. Claim: no later memory proposes trimming the slices. Phase 4 decision 5(b) and Phase 5 decision 8(b) both did.
